lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Say you have a trading idea and fifty stocks to try it on. Running them one at a time would be slow, so how do you test them all and still compare the results fairly?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'm guessing that's what BatchBacktesting does?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. Antoine read through the Python engine from the AlgoETS group and wrote up how it works. His framing is nice: a batch backtest is a small data pipeline. You choose instruments, get prices, clean them, run a strategy, and save results you can compare.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With a single instrument. A function called process_instrument picks a price source for a stock or a crypto, cleans the data, and builds a backtest. Then it stamps the instrument name and strategy name on the result so you always know which row is which.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the batch part is just doing that over and over?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Doing it in parallel. A thread pool runs several instruments at once, and the single-strategy runner defaults to four workers. Think of four cashiers serving a long line instead of one.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does a run assume about money?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It starts with a hundred thousand in cash, charges a commission of point two percent, and uses exclusive orders. Those settings sit in the constructor, so they're right there next to any return you compare.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The EMA strategy computes three moving averages, over twenty, eighty and one hundred fifty periods. Entries compare the twenty and the eighty. When it buys, it closes the previous position and sets a stop at ninety percent of the price and a target at one hundred twenty-five percent.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A CSV for each instrument, an aggregate CSV for each strategy, and optional HTML charts. The README links a published example on Apple stock, from April 2018 to April 2023. For the aggregate, Antoine suggests picking a real row by return, so the drawdown and duration you quote belong to the same run.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is that the engine keeps its assumptions visible and its outputs comparable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The full write-up has the flow diagram and links straight to the source files.
